newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Year of decision for Austria on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Year of decision for Austria on NATO.

text.p: Austria welcomed the NATO-Russia treaty on Tuesday as the birth of a new era of European security, but the ruling coalition remained divided on prospects of joining the Western alliance.

Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend, the most high-profile supporter of NATO entry, said neutral Austria could no longer remain on the sidelines and had to join the military alliance if it wanted a voice in Europe's future security.
He described the Founding Act signed in Paris as a formal end to an era of alliances forged after two world wars and the beginning of integration across the continent.

"I believe this is the only way to secure a long-lasting, freely chosen peace," said Fasslabend, who belongs to the conservative People's Party in coalition with the Social Democrats. "In this situation, we Austrians cannot and should not act as if it does not concern us, because today's event has decisive and fundamental consequences on our own security."
In his clearest remarks yet supporting NATO entry, he added: "Austria can only have a negotiating role in the future if it is a member of NATO and the WEU (the Western European Union)."

People's Party leader and Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, mindful of the sensitivity of the issue within the government, was more cautious, saying he now hoped for a vigorous debate on NATO within the coalition.
In comments seen as significant to that debate, Schuessel said the signing of the Paris treaty meant NATO was no longer a military alliance, but an all-embracing alliance.
By deploying such an argument, Schuessel's conservatives may try to come up with a formula whereby Austria could retain some notion of neutrality while being a NATO member.
That is unlikely to wash with Chancellor Viktor Klima and his Social Democrats who want Austria to remain neutral.
Klima, speaking to reporters after a weekly cabinet meeting, hailed the Paris pact as an important step in European security but made no mention of his own country's future.
Social Democrat parliamentary speaker Heinz Fischer was more direct: "There is no reason for us to change our tried and tested policies, to ditch our neutrality or to enter a military pact," he said.

Neutrality was enshrined in the constitution on the insistence of the Kremlin, which refused to pull its occupying troops out of Austria in 1955 unless the country rejected membership of military alliances. Austria was occupied by the World War Two victors after its defeat in 1945.

But conservatives insist Austria must move with the times and the near-certainty that Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary will be selected as new candidates in the first wave of enlargement at a NATO summit in Madrid in July meant Vienna had to decide as soon as possible.
If Slovenia is also included at Madrid, Austria would be almost completely encircled by NATO states.
"1997 is the year of decision for Austria," said the conservatives' Benita Ferrero-Waldner, the number two at the foreign ministry.
